Introduction

A while ago I stumbled on a wonderful acoustics education platform, acoucou.org. It is rich in content and covers a wide range of topics, with plenty of fundamentals along the way. It can show newcomers the way into acoustics, and it can also give people who work in the field fresh ideas. Today I’m sharing a selection from it.

A short history of noise control

1950: Early methods

Industrial measurements were difficult, limited by what sound level meters of the time could do.

1957: Chicago Zoning Ordinance

The first ordinance to set maximum noise levels.

1960: Measurement equipment

The rise of the environmental movement drove improvements in measurement equipment.

1968: Japan is regarded as the first country to pass environmental legislation regulating noise in working and built environments.

1972: US Noise Control Act

Aimed to give Americans an environment free from noise that jeopardizes their health and welfare.

1978: Quiet Communities Act

Promoted national and state noise control programs.

1982: The US federal government handed more of noise control policy down to local governments.

1999: WHO Guidelines for Community Noise

Community noise can cause a range of health problems: hearing impairment, startle and defense reactions, aural pain, speech interference, sleep disturbance, cardiovascular disease, annoyance and more. These health problems in turn create social problems, such as lower productivity, poorer learning, absenteeism, increased medication use and accidents.

2002: EU Directive 2002/49/EC

Directive 2002/49/EC added new provisions on noise. Community policy aims for a high level of health and environmental protection, and protection against noise is one of its objectives. The Green Paper on Future Noise Policy had already named noise as one of the main environmental problems in Europe.

2009: WHO guidelines

The WHO published the Night Noise Guidelines for Europe.

2011: WHO burden of disease

A report on the burden of disease from environmental noise, which assessed the impact of noise

in disability-adjusted life years (DALYs).

2018: WHO Environmental Noise Guidelines

The WHO’s environmental noise guidelines set out in more detail how to protect human health from harmful environmental noise.

Health effects of noise

A quick aside of my own. I don’t know much about noise control; I learned most of the above just now. The part I know a little better is the WHO’s work in recent years, because those guidelines spawned a whole wave of EU projects. Anyone who has read papers in the field will recognize the pattern: the WHO tends to turn up in the first paragraph of the introduction. To borrow an old Chinese slogan, policy is the primary productive force. It brings academia big funding, it steers where industry puts its money, and it raises public awareness of acoustics. All of that is very good news for acousticians.

A few basic acoustic concepts

We now know a bit of the history of noise control and the many ways noise can harm us. Next, a few concepts of sound propagation. Knowing how noise gets taken away is only half the story; we also need to know how it gets to us in the first place!

Sound leaves a source and reaches a listener. With nothing in the way, it travels straight to the ear. When it meets an obstacle, a whole series of more complicated phenomena appears: reflection, scattering, diffraction, refraction and so on.

Reflection

Sound striking a surface is reflected. In the figure below, sound hits a panel. If the panel is not perfectly rigid, then besides the specular reflection (red arrow), part of the sound is absorbed and part passes through the panel and keeps going (transmission). If the surface is not perfectly smooth, scattering occurs as well. Here “reflection” means specular reflection specifically: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, alpha = beta.

Think of a billiard ball bouncing off the cushion.

Scattering

Scattering, mentioned above, happens at rough surfaces. You can think of it as reflection into any direction other than the specular one. Picture water from a tap splashing out in every direction.

Transmission

Sound can pass through a boundary. That is why you can still hear the neighbors’ subwoofer with the doors and windows shut.

Diffraction

Diffraction is sound bending around an obstacle and carrying on. Low-frequency sound diffracts much more readily. In the figure below, think hiding behind the barrier keeps the sound away from you? The low frequencies still bend over the top and reach your ears. If you live next to a railway, you will hear the rumble of the trains despite the noise barrier.

Refraction

When sound passes from one medium into another, it changes direction. We all learned about the refraction of light in middle-school physics; sound refracts on the same principle.

Reverberation

This one is easy: when sound reflects many times off many surfaces, you get reverberation. The figure below shows it clearly.
